front: Name the five generic framework activities, in order.
back: **Communication → Planning → Modeling → Construction → Deployment.** Testing is *inside* Construction, not a sixth activity.

front: How many umbrella activities are there, and name four.
back: Eight. Project tracking and control, risk management, SQA, technical reviews, measurement, SCM, reusability management, work product preparation.

front: What are the three types of process pattern?
back: **Task** (one action), **Stage** (one framework activity), **Phase** (the whole project's activity sequence). Scope increases Task ⊂ Stage ⊂ Phase.

front: When is the waterfall model actually appropriate?
back: When requirements are fixed, well understood and stable, the technology is familiar, and the work is a well-defined adaptation of an existing system.

front: In the V-model, which test level pairs with architectural/system design?
back: **System testing.** The pairs are requirements↔acceptance, system design↔system test, component design↔integration test, module design↔unit test.

front: What is delivered in the first increment of the incremental model?
back: The **core product** — the essential functionality only. Customer feedback on it drives the plan for the next increment.

front: What is RAD's delivery window and what are its five phases?
back: **60–90 days.** Business modelling, data modelling, process modelling, application generation, testing and turnover.

front: Give three situations where RAD is the wrong choice.
back: The system cannot be modularised; technical risk is high; the customer and developers cannot commit to the rapid-fire timebox. (Also when high performance must be tuned at interfaces.)

front: What are Boehm's four quadrants of the spiral model?
back: 1. Determine objectives, alternatives, constraints. 2. Evaluate alternatives; identify and resolve **risks**. 3. Develop and verify the next-level product. 4. Plan the next phase.

front: What makes the spiral model unique among the classical models?
back: Explicit **risk analysis on every circuit**, and it does not stop at delivery — circuits continue through enhancement and maintenance.

front: What does the concurrent development model represent?
back: Framework activities existing **simultaneously in different states** (none, under development, awaiting changes, under review, under revision, baselined, done), with transitions triggered by events elsewhere.

front: Which model suits safety-critical software that must be mathematically verified?
back: The **formal methods model** (Cleanroom), using Z, VDM or B. Expensive, time-consuming, needs specialist training.

front: What is an aspect in AOSD?
back: A representation of a **crosscutting concern** — security, logging, persistence — that cannot be localised in any one module and is woven in at defined join points.

front: Name the Unified Process phases in order.
back: **Inception → Elaboration → Construction → Transition** (Pressman's generic UP adds Production). The executable architectural baseline is produced in **Elaboration**.

front: What are the five CMMI staged maturity levels?
back: 1 Initial, 2 Managed, 3 Defined, 4 Quantitatively Managed, 5 Optimizing. Level 3 is the first with an organisation-wide standard process; level 4 adds statistical control.

front: State the four values of the Agile Manifesto.
back: Individuals and interactions > processes and tools; working software > comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration > contract negotiation; responding to change > following a plan — while the right-hand items still have value.

front: How many agile principles are there, and what does principle 7 say?
back: **Twelve.** Principle 7: *working software is the primary measure of progress*.

front: Which agile principle defines simplicity?
back: Principle 10: *simplicity — the art of maximising the work not done — is essential*.

front: Name XP's five values.
back: Communication, simplicity, feedback, courage, respect.

front: What are XP's four framework activities?
back: **Planning** (user stories, velocity), **Design** (KISS, CRC cards, spike solutions, refactoring), **Coding** (test-first, pair programming, continuous integration), **Testing** (automated unit suite, customer acceptance tests).

front: What is a spike solution in XP?
back: A throwaway prototype built to attack one difficult design or technical problem, so that the risk is resolved before the real design commits to it.

front: Name Scrum's three roles and three artefacts.
back: Roles: **Product Owner, Scrum Master, Development Team**. Artefacts: **Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment**.

front: Give the five Scrum events with their one-month-sprint timeboxes.
back: Sprint ≤ 1 month; Sprint Planning 8 h; **Daily Scrum 15 min**; Sprint Review 4 h; Sprint Retrospective 3 h.

front: Does the Daily Scrum timebox shrink for a two-week sprint?
back: **No.** Planning, Review and Retrospective scale down (4 h / 2 h / 1.5 h), but the Daily Scrum is always 15 minutes — it re-plans the next 24 hours.

front: What are ASD's three phases?
back: **Speculation, Collaboration, Learning** (Highsmith). Mission-driven, component-based, timeboxed, risk-driven and change-tolerant.

front: What does MoSCoW stand for and which method uses it?
back: **Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time** — the prioritisation scheme of **DSDM**, which is built on the Pareto 80/20 principle.

front: Name FDD's five activities.
back: Develop an overall model; build a features list; plan by feature; design by feature; build by feature. A feature must be buildable in **two weeks or less**.

front: What two parameters select a member of the Crystal family?
back: **Team size** (colour: Clear, Yellow, Orange, Red…) and **criticality** (Comfort, Discretionary money, Essential money, Life).

front: List Lean software development's seven principles.
back: Eliminate waste; build quality in; create knowledge; defer commitment; deliver fast; respect people; optimise the whole.

front: What does Kanban limit, and what does Scrum limit?
back: **Kanban limits work in progress** (an explicit WIP cap per column, pull-based, no iterations). **Scrum limits time** (a fixed-length sprint with a committed scope).

front: Name five attributes that distinguish a WebApp.
back: Network intensiveness, concurrency, unpredictable load, continuous evolution, immediacy of delivery. (Also data/content driven, availability, security, aesthetics.)

front: Distinguish functional from non-functional requirements in one line each.
back: **Functional**: what services the system provides. **Non-functional**: constraints on how well it does it, or on the process and environment — performance, security, usability, portability, standards.

front: Give Sommerville's three classes of non-functional requirement.
back: **Product** (usability, efficiency, reliability, portability, security), **Organisational** (environmental, operational, development standards), **External** (regulatory, ethical, legislative, interoperability).

front: Name the seven requirements-engineering tasks in order.
back: Inception, Elicitation, Elaboration, Negotiation, Specification, Validation, Requirements management.

front: What are Christel and Kang's three elicitation problems?
back: Problems of **scope**, problems of **understanding**, problems of **volatility**.

front: What is FAST/JAD?
back: Facilitated Application Specification Technique — a facilitated joint meeting of customers and developers at a neutral site, producing consolidated lists of objects, services, constraints and performance criteria.

front: What three requirement bands does QFD define?
back: **Normal** (stated objectives; satisfaction proportional to fulfilment), **Expected** (so fundamental they go unmentioned), **Exciting** (beyond expectation; delight when present).

front: Difference between <<include>> and <<extend>> between use cases?
back: **include**: the base use case *always* uses the included behaviour (factored-out commonality). **extend**: the extending use case *conditionally* adds behaviour at a named extension point.

front: How many scenarios does one use case contain?
back: Many: exactly one **primary scenario** (the happy path) plus any number of alternative and exception scenarios. A scenario is one path through a use case.

front: Name the four element groups of the analysis model.
back: Scenario-based (use case, activity, swimlane), class-based (class diagram, CRC), flow-oriented (DFD, PSPEC), behavioural (state, sequence diagrams).

front: How many processes does a level 0 DFD contain?
back: Exactly **one** — the whole system as a single bubble, surrounded by external entities. That diagram is the **context diagram**.

front: What are DFD levelling and balancing?
back: **Levelling** is refining a bubble into a lower-level DFD. **Balancing** is the rule that the refined diagram's net inputs and outputs must match the parent bubble's.

front: Give the three top-level sections of an IEEE 830 SRS.
back: 1. Introduction; 2. Overall description; 3. Specific requirements (plus appendixes and index).

front: List the eight qualities of a good SRS (IEEE 830).
back: Correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, ranked for importance/stability, verifiable, modifiable, traceable.

front: "The system shall be user-friendly." Which SRS quality does this break?
back: **Verifiable** (and unambiguous) — no finite, cost-effective process can check it. Fix it by attaching a measurable criterion, e.g. "a trained operator completes a booking in under 90 s".

front: What does traceability of a requirement mean?
back: **Backward** traceable to the source or earlier document that produced it, and **forward** traceable to the design and code elements that implement it.

front: Name the four levels of software design.
back: Data/class design, architectural design, interface design, component-level design.

front: State the cohesion ladder from weakest to strongest.
back: **Coincidental, Logical, Temporal, Procedural, Communicational, Sequential, Functional.** Mnemonic: Co-Lo-Te-Pro-Com-Se-Fun.

front: State the coupling ladder from worst to best.
back: **Content, Common, External, Control, Stamp, Data.** Content (reaching into another module's internals) is worst; data (simple parameters, all used) is best.

front: How do you tell procedural from sequential cohesion?
back: Ask whether data flows. If element 2 consumes what element 1 produced → **sequential** (higher). If they merely must run in that order but pass nothing → **procedural** (lower).

front: A module is passed a whole record but uses only one field. Which coupling?
back: **Stamp coupling.** Passing just that field as a simple parameter would reduce it to **data coupling**.

front: What is the signature of control coupling?
back: A parameter that is a **switch** — a mode, type or flag — which selects which branch runs inside the callee, rather than data the callee processes.

front: What is information hiding, and why does it matter?
back: Parnas: each module conceals its design decisions behind an interface, so a change to a hidden decision stays inside that module and errors do not propagate. It is the justification for modular maintainability.

front: Is more modularity always cheaper?
back: **No.** Module cost falls with the number of modules but interface cost rises, so total cost is U-shaped with a **region of minimum cost**. Beyond it the design is overmodular.

front: Define functional independence and how it is measured.
back: Each module addresses one sub-function with simple interfaces. Measured by **high cohesion and low coupling** simultaneously.

front: Name five architectural styles.
back: Data-centred (repository/blackboard), data-flow (pipe and filter, batch sequential), call and return, object-oriented, layered.

front: What does MVC separate?
back: **Model** (data and business rules), **View** (presentation), **Controller** (interprets user input and selects model behaviour).

front: When do you use transform mapping versus transaction mapping?
back: **Transform**: the DFD is a pipeline with afferent flow, a central transform and efferent flow. **Transaction**: one incoming item fans out to several mutually exclusive action paths, giving a dispatcher module.

front: What is the scope-of-effect / scope-of-control rule?
back: The **scope of effect** of a decision (the modules it affects) should lie **within the scope of control** of the module in which the decision is made.

front: Mandel's three golden rules of interface design?
back: Place the user in control; reduce the user's memory load; make the interface consistent.

front: Quality assurance versus quality control?
back: **QA** is process-oriented and preventive (define, audit, train, measure). **QC** is product-oriented and corrective (reviews, walkthroughs, inspections, testing of specific artefacts).

front: Name McCall's five Product Operation factors.
back: Correctness, Reliability, Efficiency, Integrity, Usability.

front: Name McCall's Product Revision and Product Transition factors.
back: **Revision** (3): maintainability, flexibility, testability. **Transition** (3): portability, reusability, interoperability. Eleven factors in total, split 5-3-3.

front: List the six ISO 9126 quality characteristics.
back: Functionality, Reliability, Usability, Efficiency, Maintainability, Portability. ISO 25010 raises it to eight by adding Security and Compatibility.

front: Where do security and testability sit in ISO 9126?
back: **Security** is a sub-characteristic of **Functionality**; **testability** is a sub-characteristic of **Maintainability**. McCall instead gives them top-level factors (Integrity, Testability).

front: What does FURPS stand for?
back: **Functionality, Usability, Reliability, Performance, Supportability** (Hewlett-Packard). FURPS+ adds design, implementation, interface and physical constraints.

front: Give the three risk categories by what they threaten.
back: **Project** risks (budget, schedule, staffing, resources), **technical** risks (design, implementation, verification, maintenance), **business** risks (market, strategic, sales, management, budget).

front: What are known, predictable and unpredictable risks?
back: **Known**: found by careful evaluation of plan and environment. **Predictable**: extrapolated from past project experience. **Unpredictable**: extremely hard to identify in advance.

front: State the risk exposure formula and what it bounds.
back: $RE = P \times C$, in money. It is the expected loss, and therefore the **maximum rational spend** on mitigating that risk.

front: What does RMMM stand for?
back: **Risk Mitigation, Monitoring and Management.** Mitigate = reduce probability or impact now; monitor = watch indicators and check mitigation is applied; manage = execute the contingency plan when the trigger fires.

front: State the MTBF and availability formulas.
back: $\text{MTBF} = \text{MTTF} + \text{MTTR}$ and $\text{Availability} = \dfrac{\text{MTTF}}{\text{MTTF} + \text{MTTR}} \times 100\%$.

front: MTTF = 450 h and MTTR = 50 h. Availability?
back: MTBF = 500 h, so availability $=450/500 = \mathbf{90\%}$.

front: Reliability for constant failure rate?
back: $\lambda = 1/\text{MTTF}$ and $R(t) = e^{-\lambda t} = e^{-t/\text{MTTF}}$. POFOD, ROCOF and AVAIL are the alternative metrics.

front: Is a reliable system necessarily safe?
back: **No.** Reliability is conformance to specification over time; safety is freedom from hazardous behaviour. A system can execute a wrong specification perfectly and cause harm.

front: State the three-point size estimate formula.
back: $EV = \dfrac{a + 4m + b}{6}$ with optimistic $a$, most likely $m$, pessimistic $b$.

front: Name the five function point information domain values.
back: External Inputs, External Outputs, External Inquiries, Internal Logical Files, External Interface Files.

front: Give the FP weighting table (simple / average / complex).
State the function point formula and the range of its adjustment factor.
back: $\text{FP} = \text{UFP} \times (0.65 + 0.01\sum F_i)$ with $\sum F_i \in [0,70]$, so VAF $\in [0.65, 1.35]$ — at most ±35%.

front: How many general system characteristics are there, and what is each rated out of?
back: **Fourteen**, each rated **0 (no influence) to 5 (essential)**, giving $\sum F_i$ between 0 and 70.

front: UFP = 300 with all fourteen GSCs rated 3. Find FP.
Give the basic COCOMO effort and duration equations.
back: $E = a(\text{KLOC})^{b}$ person-months and $D = c\,E^{d}$ months, with average staff $N = E/D$.

front: Give the basic COCOMO coefficients for all three modes.
back: Organic **2.4, 1.05**; Semi-detached **3.0, 1.12**; Embedded **3.6, 1.20**. Duration: $c = 2.5$ for all three, with $d = 0.38, 0.35, 0.32$ respectively.

front: Give the intermediate COCOMO multipliers.
back: Organic **3.2**, Semi-detached **3.0**, Embedded **2.8**, with the same exponents 1.05 / 1.12 / 1.20, and $E = a(\text{KLOC})^{b} \times \text{EAF}$.

front: Compute basic COCOMO effort for 32 KLOC embedded.
back: $32 = 2^5$ so $32^{1.2} = 2^{6} = 64$, giving $E = 3.6 \times 64 = \mathbf{230.4}$ person-months.

front: What distinguishes the three COCOMO modes?
back: **Organic**: small experienced team, familiar application, flexible requirements. **Semi-detached**: mixed experience, mixed rigidity. **Embedded**: tight hardware/software/operational constraints, change very expensive.

front: Name COCOMO II's three sub-models and their size units.
back: **Application composition** (object points), **Early design** (function points, 7 effort multipliers), **Post-architecture** (KSLOC or FP, 17 multipliers and 5 scale factors).

front: State the COCOMO II post-architecture equation.
back: $\text{PM} = 2.94 \times \text{Size}^{E} \times \prod \text{EM}_i$ with $E = 0.91 + 0.01\sum SF_j$ over the five scale factors PREC, FLEX, RESL, TEAM, PMAT.

front: State Putnam's software equation and its effort form.
back: $L = C_k K^{1/3} t_d^{4/3}$, so $K = \dfrac{L^3}{C_k^{3} t_d^{4}}$. Effort varies as the **inverse fourth power of time**.

front: Schedule cut from 3 years to 2 with size unchanged. Effort multiplier?
back: $(3/2)^4 = 81/16 = \mathbf{5.06}$. Ratios need no absolute numbers: $K_1/K_2 = (t_2/t_1)^4$.

front: State the 40-20-40 rule.
back: **40% analysis and design, 20% coding, 40% testing and debugging.** Coding is the *smallest* of the three.

front: Give the four earned-value formulas.
back: $\text{SPI} = \text{BCWP}/\text{BCWS}$, $\text{CPI} = \text{BCWP}/\text{ACWP}$, $\text{SV} = \text{BCWP} - \text{BCWS}$, $\text{CV} = \text{BCWP} - \text{ACWP}$. Index above 1 is good.

front: Verification versus validation, in one question each.
back: **Verification**: are we building the product *right*? (conformance to spec, mostly static — reviews, inspections). **Validation**: are we building the *right* product? (fitness for use, dynamic — acceptance, alpha, beta).

front: State the error → fault → failure chain.
back: A human makes an **error**, which puts a **fault** (defect, bug) in the artefact, which on execution may produce a **failure** — an observed deviation from required behaviour. An unexecuted fault causes no failure.

front: What is a stub and what is a driver?
back: A **stub** replaces a module that the unit under test **calls** (below it). A **driver** replaces the module that **calls** the unit under test (above it).

front: Which integration strategy needs stubs and which needs drivers?
back: **Top-down needs stubs** (lower modules do not exist yet). **Bottom-up needs drivers** (no caller exists yet). Sandwich needs both.

front: What does regression testing re-run?
back: A representative sample of all tests, tests focused on the functions likely to be affected, and tests on the components that were actually changed — not the entire suite.

front: Give the three ways to compute cyclomatic complexity.
back: $V(G) = E - N + 2P$; $V(G) = \text{predicate nodes} + 1$; $V(G) = \text{number of regions}$ (including the unbounded one). All three must agree.

front: A flow graph has 14 edges and 11 nodes, one component. Find $V(G)$.
back: $V(G) = 14 - 11 + 2 = \mathbf{5}$, so it has 4 predicate nodes and 5 regions.

front: Does `if (a && b)` count as one predicate node?
back: **No** — a compound condition splits into **two** predicate nodes, because each simple condition is an independent decision.

front: What does $V(G)$ bound?
back: It is an **upper bound on the number of tests** needed to guarantee every statement is executed and every condition takes both values, and the **size of the basis set** of independent paths. Guideline: keep $V(G) \le 10$.

front: Must every basis path be executable?
back: **No.** The basis set is derived from the graph, not the semantics, so some paths may be infeasible; the tester substitutes realisable paths covering the same new edges.

front: How do you test a simple loop with maximum $n$ passes?
back: Skip it entirely; 1 pass; 2 passes; $m$ passes with $m < n$; and $n-1$, $n$, $n+1$ passes.

front: How does equivalence partitioning handle a range $a..b$?
back: One valid class ($a \le x \le b$) and two invalid classes ($x < a$ and $x > b$). Test one representative from each.

front: Give the four boundary-value-analysis test counts for $n$ variables.
back: Normal **$4n+1$**; robust **$6n+1$**; worst case **$5^n$**; robust worst case **$7^n$**.

front: What does cause-effect graphing add over partitioning and BVA?
back: It tests **combinations** of input conditions. Causes and effects are linked with boolean operators and constraints (E, I, O, R, M), then converted to a limited-entry decision table whose columns become test cases.

front: Alpha versus beta testing?
back: **Alpha**: at the developer's site, customer runs it, **developer present**, controlled environment, happens first. **Beta**: at the customer's site, end users run it, **developer absent**, live environment.

front: What is stress testing, and what is sensitivity testing?
back: **Stress**: abnormal quantity, frequency or volume of resource demand. **Sensitivity**: hunting the small band of input inside a valid class that causes instability or incorrect processing.

front: Name the three debugging strategies.
back: **Brute force** (dumps, traces, print statements — least efficient), **backtracking** (walk backwards from the symptom), **cause elimination** (binary partitioning of hypotheses).

front: Does condition coverage imply decision coverage?
back: **No.** For `if (a || b)`, tests (T,F) and (F,T) give full condition coverage but both take the true branch. That gap is why condition/decision coverage and MC/DC exist.

front: Give the IEEE definition of a baseline.
back: A specification or product that has been **formally reviewed and agreed upon**, that thereafter serves as the **basis for further development**, and that can be **changed only through formal change control procedures**.

front: What counts as a software configuration item?
back: Any information item under configuration control: specifications, plans, design documents, source code, test plans and cases, executables, databases, manuals, change requests — and increasingly the build tools themselves.

front: Name the five SCM tasks.
back: Identification, version control, change control, configuration auditing, status reporting (status accounting).

front: Version, revision, variant, release — distinguish them.
back: **Version**: any distinguishable instance. **Revision**: corrects or improves and is meant to **replace** its predecessor. **Variant**: functionally equivalent for a different environment and **co-exists**. **Release**: a version shipped to customers.

front: Order the change control steps for a baselined item.
back: Change request → evaluation and **change report** → **CCA/CCB decision** → **ECO** → check out → make change → review and audit → check in → baseline for testing → promote → release.

front: What level of change control applies before an item is baselined?
back: **Informal** — the developer simply makes the change. Project-level control applies once baselined, formal control with a CCB once released.

front: What does a configuration audit ask that a technical review does not?
back: Was the change in the ECO actually made and were extra modifications added? Was an FTR held? Were SCM procedures followed? Were all related SCIs updated?

front: Name the four maintenance categories and their rough shares.
back: **Perfective ~50%**, adaptive ~25%, corrective ~21%, preventive ~4%. Enhancement dominates — corrective is not the largest.

front: Give Lehman's first two laws of software evolution.
back: 1. **Continuing change** — an E-type program must be continually adapted or become less satisfactory. 2. **Increasing complexity** — complexity rises as it evolves unless work is done to reduce it.

front: What is MTTC?
back: **Mean time to change** — the average time to analyse a change request, design the modification, implement it, test it and distribute it. It is the standard maintainability metric.

front: Name the three levels of software reuse.
back: Application system reuse (COTS, product lines), component reuse (subsystems and components), object and function reuse (classes, library functions).

front: Name the three steps of component-based reuse and the preferred wrapping technique.
back: Qualification, adaptation, composition (plus update). **Black-box wrapping** — changing only the interface — is preferred over grey-box and white-box wrapping.

front: Reuse break-even: build premium $p$, per-reuse cost $r$ (as multiples of single-use cost $C$).
back: $p + rn = n \Rightarrow n = \dfrac{p}{1-r}$. With $p = 1.5$ and $r = 0.2$, $n = 1.875$, so the **second** use is the first profitable one.

front: Name the six activities of the software re-engineering process model.
back: Inventory analysis, document restructuring, reverse engineering, code restructuring, data restructuring, forward engineering.

front: Define reverse engineering precisely.
back: Analysing a program to create a representation of it at a **higher level of abstraction** than the source code — design recovery. It changes nothing in the system.

front: How do reverse engineering, forward engineering, restructuring and re-engineering differ?
back: Abstraction goes **up** (reverse), **down** (forward), **sideways** (restructuring, behaviour preserved) and **up then down** (re-engineering, which contains reverse engineering).
